answers.Q1: A `-k`/node-id partial run would rewrite the generated spec with only the collected tests, silently deleting every scenario that did not run. The project cares because the generated spec is the test-suite contract/source of truth; silently losing its unrun scenarios makes that contract incomplete and misleading. Users must either run the full suite or explicitly opt into an in-place merge.
answers.Q2: Ordering test execution would create runtime-coupled tests: they could not safely run alone or in parallel, and could pass for the wrong reasons. `depends_on` is therefore a reader/reporting graph (and an earlier failed prerequisite can mark a later scenario blocked), not a mechanism for reordering pytest execution.
answers.Q3: A function run by most scenarios conveys no useful narrowing information: execution is not proof that the test checks that function, and the honest set of tests that would fail is usually much smaller. Listing the 47 scenarios was repeated noise shaped like evidence; in measurement it caused an agent to claim 87 tests would fail when none would, worse than omitting the map.
answers.Q4: Every `depends_on` emitted in a generated spec names a scenario that exists, including when parametrized scenario aliases collide with another scenario id.
answers.Q5: The user gets a CI/PR Markdown report that takes scenario status from the generated spec’s `status:` tags and correctly reports dependency-blocked scenarios, including cascading blocks, as not run.
answers.Q9: They are opt-in because specdeck must be safe to add to an existing suite: a tool that makes someone else’s previously passing build fail on installation will be removed. Gates let teams deliberately turn informational traceability/validation findings into CI policy.
answers.Q10: It protects the explicit rule that only a prerequisite that ran earlier can block a scenario; a failed prerequisite that runs later does not prevent the scenario from running and failing independently. The project cares because people and agents otherwise apply the intuitive but wrong “anything upstream failed means blocked” rule, which badly misclassifies root failures versus blocked fallout.

answers.Q1: A selected run (for example, `-k test_one`) would rewrite the generated spec with only the selected tests, silently deleting every unselected scenario. Users would get an incomplete, misleading source-of-truth document and lose prior scenario/status information; specdeck therefore refuses the rewrite unless they explicitly request a preserving merge.
answers.Q2: `depends_on` must not make tests runtime-coupled or let specdeck override pytest’s natural collection/execution order. Specdeck uses the relationship to present and interpret results—only an already-run failed prerequisite can block a later scenario—but never schedules tests from it, so tests still run independently and a prerequisite that happens later cannot change an earlier test’s execution.
answers.Q3: Listing the scenarios would imply that they are a useful, bounded answer to “which tests could break if this function changes.” For a near-universal hook/configuration/constructor, execution by many tests is not discriminating, and only a much smaller unknown subset may actually check it; the count avoids a long, misleading list and tells the agent not to infer that all those scenarios are likely failures.
answers.Q4: Specdeck guarantees that a `depends_on` alias for a parametrized scenario resolves to its real generated scenario ids—even when a generated id is renamed because it collides—so the emitted spec never contains a dangling dependency.
answers.Q5: The user gets a PR report based on the recorded `status:` tags that correctly identifies skipped downstream scenarios as blocked, including cascading blockage, rather than treating them as ordinary skips or inventing statuses from some other source.
answers.Q9: Because specdeck is intended to be safe to add to an existing local workflow or CI suite: it should report requirements/spec problems without unexpectedly turning previously green builds red. Failing on those findings is a policy decision, so users opt into it with a gate when they are ready to enforce it.
answers.Q10: It protects the coding-agent document’s exact explanation that `depends_on` is documentation/reporting order, does not reorder tests, and blocks only after an earlier prerequisite fails; a later failed dependency does not skip the scenario. The project cares because the wrong blocking interpretation caused agents to confuse root failures with blocked failures—measured root-cause classification fell from 100% to 70%.

answers.Q1: A `-k`/partial run could overwrite the full spec with only the selected tests, silently deleting all deselected scenarios. The project cares because the generated spec is a record of the suite, not merely of the last selection; users must explicitly choose `--specdeck-merge` to update only what ran while retaining the rest.
answers.Q2: Test execution remains pytest’s responsibility: reordering tests can change fixture/state behavior, conflict with pytest’s own ordering, parallelism, or selection rules, and can conceal real failures. `depends_on` is therefore documentary/reporting information (with blocking interpreted only from an earlier run), not an instruction to alter execution order.
answers.Q3: A hub function exercised by most scenarios does not identify the tests relevant to a particular change; the long, identical list is noise that readers mistake for evidence. Measurement showed agents given such a list answered with nearly every test name even when none was the answer, so the document reports a count and preserves lists only where they are discriminating.
answers.Q4: The project guarantees that every emitted `depends_on` reference resolves to an actual final scenario id, even when parametrization and id de-duplication collide.
answers.Q5: The user gets a CI/PR report whose scenario statuses come from the generated spec’s status tags, correctly labels skipped dependents as blocked through the full dependency cascade regardless of document order, and counts untagged/pending scenarios as not run.
answers.Q9: Because specdeck must be safe to add to an existing test suite: reporting, requirements metadata, or a generated-spec issue must not unexpectedly turn a formerly green suite red. Users opt into gates when they deliberately want those quality policies enforced in CI.
answers.Q10: It protects the coding-agent document’s explicit explanation that `depends_on` never reorders tests and blocks a scenario only when its prerequisite ran earlier and failed; a prerequisite that runs later does not block it. The project cares because testing showed readers otherwise apply the wrong blocking rule, badly misclassifying failures versus blocked work.
